prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map places the reclining person and the patterned cushion/blanket directly in front of the camera wearer, with the person roughly 0.5–1.0 m away and the surrounding surface about 0.4–1.2 m away; the dark upper background appears farther away, likely beyond 1.5–2 m. The person remains near the lower middle of all five frames, shifts from slightly left to right and back toward center-right, and appears at broadly similar distance rather than clearly approaching or retreating. The bright lower edge is extremely near—probably within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach—but is partly outside the field of view; the person is plausibly within extended reach, while no other person is visible. This map makes foreground/background separation and the partial occlusion of the person by the near lower-edge surface clearer than RGB alone, but its smooth halos, saturated white regions, and monocular scale make exact metre estimates and small depth changes unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates one person in frames 1, 2, and 5 and a large curved object behind or around them in frames 1–2; the masks place the person in the lower central area, roughly 0.5–1.0 m from the camera, with the surrounding object at a similar or slightly greater distance. In frames 1–2 the person overlaps and occludes part of that object, while the object extends farther left and right; in frame 5 only the person’s right-side portion is segmented, suggesting cropping or missed regions. The masks clarify object boundaries and overlap that are difficult to distinguish in the dark RGB, but frame 3 has no detections and frame 4 labels a large background/cover region as “pizzan,” which is visibly unreliable. Because segmentation contains no direct depth or gaze information, distances, arm’s reach, and whether the person faces or looks toward the camera can only be approximated from the aligned RGB; the blurred face appears generally oriented toward the camera in several frames, without a reliable eye-direction estimate.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects a partial body skeleton only in frame 1 and a short, nearly horizontal limb or hand-related chain in frame 2; both lie in the lower-left to lower-middle foreground, aligned with the nearby reclining person at roughly 0.5–1.0 m. In frame 1 the detected joints indicate a bent, partly side-on posture, with one segment extending upward, but the head, torso, and most limbs are missing, so facing direction and gaze toward the camera cannot be established reliably. The frame-2 chain shifts rightward and becomes almost horizontal, which may reflect body movement or merely unstable keypoint detection; frames 3–5 contain no usable pose points, so approach, retreat, or turning cannot be tracked. Pose makes limb articulation and joint placement more explicit than the dark RGB where detected, but severe occlusion, cropping, blur, and missing keypoints make reach estimates unreliable; the visible detected limbs appear near enough to the person’s surrounding surface, while their reach relative to the camera wearer cannot be determined precisely.
